choices.text: A confirmed queen room at a 4.0-rated hotel for $166 per night, with a pool, hot tub, and fitness room.
A confirmed king room at a 4.7-rated hotel for $174 per night, with a pool, hot tub, and fitness room.
A confirmed queen room at a 4.8-rated hotel for $168 per night, with a pool and fitness room but no hot tub.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Without history, A's lower price and complete amenity set must be weighed against B's much higher customer rating and larger bed, with no generally dominant answer. History supplies two scoped soft rules that resolve the tradeoff: ratings at or above 4.0 are sufficient, and a king is not an automatic replacement for an available queen.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the confirmed queen room in option A.
probes.label_rationale: A preserves Kara's recurring queen default when it is selectable while also meeting the full pool, hot-tub, and fitness bundle at the lower price. The 4.0 rating satisfies her usual rating floor; the higher scores in B and C are bonuses, not a reason to replace a suitable queen with a king or to give up the hot tub. Sessions s0005, s0011, and s0057 establish the selectable-queen pattern across Denver, Blue Ridge, and Denver again; s0052 shows that a king is acceptable in context, but not a standing upgrade rule.
probes.query: Kara and her partner are choosing a refundable two-night hotel for a low-key recovery weekend. They need one room, but this trip has no separate-bed request or stated bed size. Each option is nine minutes from the trailhead, includes an in-room coffee maker and mini-fridge, and has identical cancellation terms. Customer ratings are from the same source. Which option should lead?

choices.text: A 4.4-rated confirmed queen room with an in-room coffee maker and mini-fridge, plus a pool and hot tub but no fitness room.
A 4.6-rated confirmed king room with lobby coffee and no in-room refrigerator, plus a pool, hot tub, and fitness room.
A 4.8-rated confirmed queen room with an in-room coffee maker and mini-fridge plus fitness access, but no pool or hot tub.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The query alone leaves a genuine conflict among a queen with room conveniences, a king with the complete recovery bundle, and a higher-rated queen with only fitness. The history is needed to combine the queen default with the early-morning coffee/fridge preference while treating the all-three recovery bundle as a strong but soft consideration rather than a mandatory rule.
probes.gold_action: Hold option A, the confirmed queen room with in-room coffee and a mini-fridge.
probes.label_rationale: A is the best balanced fit for an early-morning work stay: it keeps the selectable queen and confirmed in-room coffee/fridge setup while retaining two recovery amenities. B's complete recovery bundle is a close match, but it trades away both in-room routine amenities and the queen; C keeps the room basics but gives up both pool and hot tub. In s0006 Kara would not switch without a queen and fridge, s0022 made queen-plus-fridge confirmation decisive against an attached alternative, and s0053 and s0083 again required confirmation of a real queen together with coffee and fridge across separate trips.
probes.query: For a three-night solo teaching stay in Spokane, Kara will have early morning setup and long teaching days. Three refundable hotels are the same price and are each a six-minute covered walk from the training site. No amenity is mandatory for this trip. Which room should be held?

choices.text: A confirmed king studio at a 4.1-rated hotel for $184 per night, reached by a seven-minute covered walk.
A confirmed two-double room at a 4.7-rated hotel for $184 per night, also reached by a seven-minute covered walk.
A confirmed king studio at a 4.8-rated hotel for $174 per night, reached by a 17-minute direct hotel shuttle.

probes.difficulty_rationale: A query-only planner can reasonably prefer B's higher rating or C's higher rating and lower price, while another may prefer A's one larger bed and shorter access. History is required to apply the boundary correctly: Kara prefers a queen when available, but a confirmed king is acceptable when it is the practical one-bed alternative and should not be treated like an unwanted double-bed setup.
probes.gold_action: Lead with option A, the confirmed king studio.
probes.label_rationale: With no queen available, the confirmed king in A is an allowed one-bed substitute and is preferable to B's two-double setup. Its 4.1 rating clears Kara's normal quality floor, and its short covered walk avoids C's longer shuttle despite C's rating and savings. Session s0011 says to skip doubles when one larger bed is appropriate, s0047 specifies queen rather than doubles, s0089 explicitly treats a king as fine before two doubles, and s0098 again distinguishes a queen studio from a two-double room.
probes.query: Kara is traveling solo for a three-night Harrisburg seminar, and trip confirmation requires a refundable room hold today. No queen rooms remain at any of the three hotels, and no separate-bed arrangement has been requested. All three rooms have an in-room coffee maker, mini-fridge, pool, hot tub, fitness access, and the same cancellation terms. Which hold should lead?
